patient.chief_complaint: New drooping of right eyelid and double vision in a patient known to have Graves' disease and thyroid eye disease
patient.history_present_illness:
A 38-year-old East Asian woman with known Graves' disease (on methimazole) and thyroid-associated ophthalmopathy was admitted after developing new right-sided eyelid droop and double vision over the preceding 6 weeks. She had been diagnosed with Graves' disease 14 months ago after presenting to her primary care physician with palpitations, heat intolerance, and unintentional 5 kg weight loss. Thyroid function confirmed TSH suppression with elevated free T4 and T3; TRAb was markedly positive. She was started on methimazole. Eight months ago, mild proptosis was noted bilaterally (right greater than left) by her ophthalmologist, attributed to thyroid-associated ophthalmopathy (clinical activity score 3/7). Selenium was added and artificial tears prescribed. She was told that some degree of eyelid abnormality can occur in thyroid eye disease.

However, over the past 6 weeks she developed a new right eyelid droop she had NOT had before, with a distinctly different character than her proptosis: the lid drooping was worse in the evening and after prolonged activities, and completely resolved each morning after a night of sleep. She also developed intermittent horizontal double vision that she localized to rightward gaze. Both the ptosis and the diplopia were worse after a long day of teaching and resolved after rest. She denied new proptosis, significant orbital pain, or corneal irritation symptoms beyond baseline. She also noticed jaw fatigue when eating tougher foods and her husband noted her voice became nasal after prolonged conversations.

Her endocrinologist initially attributed the new eyelid findings to progressive thyroid eye disease and admitted her for IV glucocorticoids. Neurology was consulted because the admitting team found the ptosis to be fatigable on sustained upgaze — a pattern inconsistent with the restrictive lid retraction or mechanical proptosis-related changes of thyroid eye disease, which are non-fatigable. Neurology examination confirmed fatigable ptosis with complete recovery after rest, proximal limb weakness, and nasal voice after sustained speech — raising concern for a neuromuscular junction disorder coexisting with the established thyroid autoimmunity.

output.query: myasthenia gravis autoimmune thyroid disease Graves coexistence clinical management

results.title: Coexistence of primary NMJ autoimmunity and autoimmune thyroid disease: clinical features and shared mechanisms
results.finding: Autoimmune thyroid disease (Graves' or Hashimoto's) coexists with primary NMJ autoimmunity in approximately 5-10% of patients with the latter; AChR-positive postsynaptic NMJ disease is the most common antibody subtype in this overlap; both conditions share HLA-DR3 susceptibility and polyclonal B-cell activation. TRAb-positive Graves' disease can cause thyroid orbitopathy with proptosis and lid retraction — clinically distinct from the fatigable ptosis of NMJ disease; differentiating the two requires NMJ electrophysiology and antibody testing rather than relying on thyroid antibody status alone.

results.title: Thyroid eye disease vs ocular myasthenia gravis: clinical differentiation and diagnostic approach
results.finding: Thyroid eye disease (TAO) causes non-fatigable, restrictive ophthalmoplegia with forced duction test resistance; myasthenia gravis causes fatigable, non-restrictive diplopia and ptosis that improves with rest. Both can coexist in the same patient; an ice pack test positive for ptosis improvement and an RNS decrement >10% differentiate MG-related from TAO-related ocular signs. Thyroid function normalization does not reliably resolve MG symptoms.

results.title: Thyrotoxic myopathy and neuromuscular junction disorders: differential diagnosis and overlap
results.finding: Thyrotoxic myopathy occurs in up to 70% of patients with hyperthyroidism and manifests as proximal limb weakness without fatigability, normal NMJ electrophysiology, and elevated creatine kinase in severe cases; it resolves with thyroid function normalization. RNS decrement and AChR seropositivity are not features of thyrotoxic myopathy and indicate a concurrent NMJ disorder when present.

results.title: Thymoma and thyroid autoimmunity in myasthenia gravis
results.finding: Thymoma-associated MG occurs in approximately 10-15% of generalized AChR-positive MG; thymic hyperplasia (not thymoma) is common in young AChR-positive females and can appear as anterior mediastinal soft tissue on CT. Beta-blockers used for symptomatic management of hyperthyroidism have a controversial interaction with MG — generally considered safe at standard doses but should be used with monitoring for MG worsening.

output.summary: MG and autoimmune thyroid disease (Graves' or Hashimoto's) coexist in 5-10% of MG patients, sharing immunological risk factors. Thyroid eye disease and ocular MG cause clinically overlapping ocular signs but differ fundamentally in mechanism: TAO is restrictive (non-fatigable), MG is NMJ-mediated (fatigable, positive ice pack test, positive RNS). Thyrotoxic myopathy produces proximal weakness without NMJ decrement. Positive AChR antibodies and RNS decrement >10% are specific for MG and are not caused by thyroid disease. Thymoma screening with CT chest is mandatory in confirmed AChR-positive MG regardless of thyroid status. Evidence level: multiple cohort studies and expert consensus.

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: Myasthenia gravis, AChR antibody-positive, generalized (MGFA Class II-III), with comorbid autoimmune thyroid disease (Graves' disease, TRAb-positive) and thyroid-associated ophthalmopathy

differential.diagnosis: Thyroid eye disease (TAO) as sole explanation for ocular signs
differential.key_features: Pre-existing Graves' disease with proptosis and prior ophthalmology attribution makes TAO the leading initial working hypothesis; distinguished from MG by fatigable (not restrictive) character of ptosis and positive ice pack test.
Persistent hyperthyroidism (TSH 0.08, elevated FT3/FT4) can cause proximal muscle weakness; however, thyrotoxic myopathy does not produce RNS decrement or AChR positivity — both present here.
LEMS gives proximal weakness that transiently improves with exercise and shows >100% facilitation on high-rate RNS; here facilitation absent, AChR positive, no SCLC risk factors.
Ocular-only MG remains possible but proximal limb weakness (shoulders 4/5, hip flexors 4+/5) and bulbar signs (nasal voice, jaw fatigue) indicate generalized involvement — MGFA Class II-III.
Fluctuating, fatigable ophthalmoplegia with positive ice pack test and RNS decrement are not features of structural brainstem or cranial nerve disease; no MRI abnormality.

optimal_actions.action: Check drug interactions for MG-exacerbating drugs; specifically flag propranolol use in MG and screen for aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones, telithromycin, IV magnesium
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Propranolol (beta-blocker for hyperthyroidism) requires monitoring in MG — generally safe but should be reassessed once thyroid control achieved; aminoglycosides/fluoroquinolones/telithromycin/IV magnesium contraindicated; corticosteroids for TAO may paradoxically worsen MG at initiation

useless_tools.rationale: MG is a peripheral neuromuscular junction disorder; EEG has no diagnostic role.
CSF analysis has no role in MG; LP risks complications without diagnostic yield.
Advanced imaging (PET, MR spectroscopy, perfusion) is not indicated for MG diagnosis or staging; CT chest covers thymoma screening.
Brain MRI is non-contributory once NMJ etiology is established by RNS decrement and AChR positivity; reserve for cases where a CNS/brainstem cause is genuinely entertained and not yet excluded.

sequence_constraints.reason: Order AChR serology first to stratify antibody status; electrodiagnostic testing contextualizes serological findings and guides whether single-fiber EMG is needed.

critical_actions: Confirm AChR antibody positivity to establish MG as a diagnosis independent of thyroid status — do not attribute all ocular and limb findings to thyroid disease
Obtain TSH, free T4, free T3, TRAb, and anti-TPO to characterize thyroid autoimmune status and distinguish Graves' from Hashimoto's in case of hypothyroid myopathy consideration
CT chest with contrast for thymoma screening — required in all confirmed AChR-positive MG regardless of thyroid comorbidity

Communicate to ophthalmology that the planned IV glucocorticoids for TAO carry a risk of paradoxical MG worsening — initiate pyridostigmine bridge before steroids and ensure inpatient respiratory monitoring during steroid initiation
Assess whether propranolol (used for Graves' tachycardia) is contributing to or risking MG symptoms — reassess beta-blocker need once thyroid function normalizes
Document baseline respiratory function (FVC, NIF) before steroid initiation
contraindicated_actions: Do NOT prescribe aminoglycoside antibiotics (gentamicin, tobramycin, amikacin) — risk of precipitating myasthenic crisis
Do NOT prescribe fluoroquinolones (ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin, moxifloxacin) — FDA black-box warning for MG exacerbation
Do NOT prescribe telithromycin — contraindicated in MG
Do NOT administer IV magnesium — blocks NMJ transmission and can precipitate myasthenic crisis
Do NOT use non-depolarizing neuromuscular blockers without anaesthesia/MG-aware dosing protocols

Do NOT initiate high-dose corticosteroids (including for TAO) without hospitalization, pyridostigmine bridge, and respiratory monitoring — risk of paradoxical MG worsening at days 5-10 of steroid initiation

Do NOT attribute all ocular signs (ptosis, diplopia) to thyroid eye disease and withhold NMJ evaluation — coexistence of both conditions in the same patient is well documented and requires independent workup of each process
key_reasoning_points: Fatigable ptosis (worsens with sustained upgaze, resolves with rest and ice pack) is the signature of NMJ-mediated weakness and is mechanistically distinct from the non-fatigable lid retraction or proptosis of thyroid eye disease — the quality of fatigability, not the mere presence of lid/eye signs, drives the differential.

AChR antibody positivity and RNS decrement >10% confirm MG as a second coexisting autoimmune process, independent of Graves' disease serology; TRAb positivity and suppressed TSH confirm the thyroid disease but do NOT explain the NMJ findings.

Thyrotoxic myopathy (a common confounder in active hyperthyroidism) produces proximal weakness without RNS decrement and without AChR seropositivity — its presence does not exclude concurrent MG but it should not anchor the diagnosis away from the NMJ.

The planned IV glucocorticoid therapy for TAO introduces a critical management interaction: steroids used for thyroid eye disease carry a paradoxical risk of transiently worsening MG in the first 1-2 weeks — both teams must coordinate, and pyridostigmine should be established before steroid initiation with respiratory monitoring in place.

Propranolol (prescribed for Graves'-related tachycardia) is generally safe in MG at standard doses but should be flagged — it is the only beta-blocker on the medication list, and escalating doses or switching to non-selective agents without awareness of the MG diagnosis creates risk; once hyperthyroidism is controlled, need for beta-blockade should be reassessed.

CT chest for thymoma screening is non-negotiable in all confirmed AChR-positive MG, even when the anterior mediastinal appearance is non-thymomatous — thymic hyperplasia is a common CT finding in young AChR-positive women and does not require further immediate action, but must be documented and the absence of a discrete encapsulated mass noted.

red_herrings.data_point: Pre-existing Graves' disease with TRAb 8.4 IU/L, bilateral proptosis (Hertel right 3 mm, left 2 mm), and ophthalmology documentation of thyroid-associated ophthalmopathy (CAS 3/7)
red_herrings.location: past medical history and neurological exam
red_herrings.intended_effect: Anchor all ocular signs (ptosis, diplopia) to thyroid eye disease and attribute limb weakness to thyrotoxic myopathy — proceeding to IV glucocorticoids for TAO without NMJ evaluation.
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Fatigable ptosis with positive ice pack test, RNS decrement >10%, and AChR positivity establish coexisting MG independent of TAO; both diagnoses are present simultaneously and require separate management strategies.

red_herrings.data_point: TSH 0.08 mIU/L, free T4 22.4 pmol/L, free T3 7.8 pmol/L — active hyperthyroidism at time of presentation
red_herrings.intended_effect: Attribute proximal limb weakness entirely to thyrotoxic myopathy (common in active Graves' disease) and defer MG workup until thyroid function normalizes.
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Thyrotoxic myopathy does not produce RNS decrement or AChR seropositivity; these findings require MG workup regardless of thyroid status. Both conditions must be diagnosed and treated concurrently.

red_herrings.data_point: Propranolol 20 mg twice daily on medication list
red_herrings.intended_effect: Attribute new-onset limb weakness or worsening fatigue to beta-blocker side effects rather than MG.
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Beta-blockers can contribute to fatigue but do not produce fatigable ptosis, diplopia, positive ice pack test, or RNS decrement; AChR seropositivity and NMJ electrophysiology establish MG as the primary neuromuscular diagnosis.

metadata.real_seed_note: Demographics and subtype loosely seeded from Patient 2 in PMC5589050 (66-year-old Cantonese female with Graves' + ocular MG + thymoma, PMID 28882932). Case demographics, disease severity, thymic finding, and clinical complexity differ substantially: this case features a 38-year-old East Asian woman with generalized (not purely ocular) MG, no discrete thymoma (thymic hyperplasia only), active hyperthyroidism with thyrotoxic myopathy as additional red herring, and propranolol interaction as a second red herring.
metadata.difficulty_description: Moderate: known Graves' disease with thyroid eye disease creates strong anchoring on TAO as sole explanation for all ocular signs; active hyperthyroidism adds thyrotoxic myopathy as a competing explanation for proximal weakness; propranolol on medication list is a third decoy; RNS decrement and AChR positivity disentangle the overlapping diagnoses
metadata.difficulty_rationale: 5 required tools, 3 red herrings (TAO anchoring, thyrotoxic myopathy, propranolol attribution), requires synthesis across MG serology + thyroid labs + NMJ electrophysiology + medication review to disentangle two coexisting autoimmune processes
